title: Language and Power
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about how language is never neutral -- how society judges people by the way they speak, why 'correct' English is really a question of power, and what linguistic justice demands.
competenceGoals: discuss and elaborate on how language is connected to power and social inequality
analyze language attitudes and their consequences for individuals and groups

content.content:
## Language, Power, and Inequality

Language is never neutral. The way you speak marks you as belonging to particular social groups, and society quietly assigns different levels of prestige to different ways of speaking. These attitudes have real consequences -- they can open doors or close them, include people or exclude them, empower communities or push them to the margins.

Who decides what counts as "correct" language? There is a persistent belief that some forms of language are "proper" or "educated" while others are "sloppy" or "uneducated." But from a linguistic point of view, all natural varieties of language are systematic, rule-governed, and capable of expressing complex thought. The varieties considered "standard" or "prestigious" are not linguistically superior -- they are simply the varieties spoken by those who hold social and economic power. Consider: in England, RP is widely perceived as more intelligent than Cockney or Brummie; in the USA, African American Vernacular English is stigmatised despite being fully systematic; in Norway, some dialects carry more prestige than others. The key insight is that **language prejudice is really social prejudice** -- when people judge a way of speaking, they are usually judging the people who speak that way.

## Standard Language and Hidden Ideology

To understand how this works, we need two concepts. A **standard language** is a variety that has been *codified* -- given official grammar rules, dictionaries, and spelling -- and that is used in education, government, and media, and generally perceived as "correct." A **language ideology** is a set of beliefs about language that reflects the social, political, and economic interests of particular groups, often presented as common sense while actually serving to maintain existing power structures.

The most powerful of these is **standard language ideology**: the belief that there is one correct way to speak and write, and that this standard is inherently better than non-standard varieties. This ideology presents the standard as neutral and natural when it is actually a social construct; it stigmatises non-standard speakers as uneducated; it benefits speakers of the standard variety in education and employment; and it ignores the systematic, rule-governed nature of non-standard varieties.

A related distinction is between **prescriptivism** and **descriptivism**. Prescriptivism says language should follow established rules and that deviations are errors ("You should say 'whom,' not 'who'"). Descriptivism observes and documents how language is *actually* used, without judging correctness ("Speakers increasingly use 'who' in all positions"). Most modern linguists are descriptivists, while public discourse about language tends to be prescriptivist. The consequences of these attitudes are serious. Picture three scenarios: a job applicant with a strong regional accent is not hired despite the best qualifications; a student whose first language is not English is placed in a lower academic track; a politician is mocked for using working-class grammar. In every case, language is being used as a *proxy* for social class, intelligence, or competence. The discrimination is not really about language at all -- it is about the social groups associated with particular ways of speaking.

questions.task: Why are 'standard' varieties of a language considered correct?

options.text: Because they are objectively clearer and more logical
Because they have more words
Because they are older than all other varieties
Because they are spoken by those who hold social and economic power, not because they are linguistically superior

questions.solution: Standard varieties are not linguistically superior; they are simply spoken by powerful groups. Language prejudice functions as social prejudice.

questions.task: What is the difference between prescriptivism and descriptivism?

options.text: Prescriptivism judges language by rules; descriptivism documents how language is actually used
Prescriptivism studies how people speak; descriptivism makes rules
They mean exactly the same thing
Neither concerns language

questions.solution: Prescriptivism focuses on rules and 'correctness'; descriptivism observes actual usage without judgement. Most modern linguists are descriptivists.

questions.task: When language attitudes lead to job discrimination, what is really happening?

options.text: The applicant genuinely cannot communicate
Language is being used as a proxy for social class or competence
Accent objectively measures intelligence
The employer is being scientific

questions.solution: Accent-based hiring discrimination uses language as a stand-in for class and competence. The discrimination is about social groups, not actual ability -- research shows non-standard speakers are unfairly underrated.

options.text: It proves one variety is biologically superior
It treats all varieties as equal
It presents one variety as inherently correct, a social construct disguised as common sense
It has no effect on society

questions.solution: Standard language ideology presents the standard as neutral and natural when it is a social construct, stigmatising non-standard speakers and benefiting those who speak the standard.

content.content:
## Language Rights and Linguistic Justice

Recognising that language discrimination is a form of social injustice has led to growing attention to **language rights** -- the rights of individuals and communities to use, maintain, and develop their languages without facing discrimination. These include the right to use one's language in private life, the right to education in one's language (especially in the early years), the right to public services like healthcare and legal proceedings in a language one understands, and the right to maintain and develop one's language through media and literature.

International frameworks have begun to enshrine these rights: the **Universal Declaration of Linguistic Rights** (1996) asserts that all language communities have equal rights, the **European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages** (1992) commits states to protecting minority languages, and the **UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples** (2007) recognises indigenous language rights.

The broader principle is **linguistic justice**, which asks who benefits and who is disadvantaged by current language arrangements. When English is the default of international business and science, native English speakers enjoy an automatic advantage. When a country conducts all official business in one language, speakers of minority languages are disadvantaged. Achieving linguistic justice means balancing the practical need for a common language against respect for diversity and minority speakers' rights. A few terms sharpen the picture: **language discrimination** (linguicism) is discrimination based on language or dialect; **prestige variety** is a variety associated with status and power; and intriguingly, **covert prestige** is the hidden prestige non-standard varieties carry within their own communities -- speaking with a strong local accent may win respect among peers even when wider society stigmatises it. The deepest point stands firm: non-standard varieties are linguistically equal to standard ones -- systematic, rule-governed, and fully expressive.

questions.task: What does the principle of 'linguistic justice' ask us to consider?

options.text: Which language is grammatically best
How to make everyone speak English
Why dialects should be banned
Who benefits and who is disadvantaged by current language arrangements

questions.solution: Linguistic justice asks who benefits and who loses from language arrangements -- for example, the automatic advantage native English speakers gain when English is the global default.

options.text: The hidden prestige a non-standard variety carries within its own community
The official prestige of the standard language
The prestige of writing in Latin
A type of language discrimination

questions.solution: Covert prestige is the respect a non-standard variety commands among its own speakers -- a strong local accent may carry prestige with peers even while wider society stigmatises it.

questions.task: Which international framework asserts that all language communities have equal rights?

options.text: The Great Vowel Shift
The Universal Declaration of Linguistic Rights (1996)
Webster's Dictionary
The Norman Conquest

questions.solution: The Universal Declaration of Linguistic Rights (1996) asserts equal rights for all language communities, alongside frameworks like the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages.

questions.task: What is the linguistic truth about non-standard varieties?

options.text: They have no grammar and cannot express complex ideas
They are simply lazy versions of the standard
They are systematic, rule-governed, and fully expressive -- equal to standard varieties
They are spoken only by uneducated people

questions.solution: Non-standard varieties are linguistically equal to standard ones -- they have their own systematic rules and can express any thought. The stigma against them is social, not linguistic.

content.content:
## Summary

Language is never neutral -- different ways of speaking carry different levels of social prestige. **Standard language ideology** presents one variety as inherently correct, but standards are social constructs that reflect power structures, and **language prejudice functions as social prejudice** (class, race, region). This discrimination has real consequences in employment, education, and public life. The distinction between **prescriptivism** (rules and correctness) and **descriptivism** (documenting actual usage) clarifies how linguists differ from popular discourse. Growing attention to **language rights** and **linguistic justice** -- supported by frameworks like the Universal Declaration of Linguistic Rights -- asks who benefits and who is disadvantaged by language arrangements. The underlying truth never changes: non-standard varieties are linguistically equal to standard ones, systematic and fully expressive.
